label: Products: ethanol + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O → C1; curly: bond C1–Br → Br
what the engine says happens: O's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: O acts as a nucleophile. Heterolytic fission: the C1–Br bond breaks and both electrons go to Br, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. Both happen at once on the same carbon: a concerted, one-step substitution (SN2). The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, so the configuration is inverted.
explanation shown to students: A curly arrow shows a pair of electrons moving. The nucleophile's lone pair forms the new C–O bond; because carbon can't have five bonds, the C–Br bond breaks in the same step, its pair going to bromine (more electronegative), which leaves as Br⁻.

label: Tertiary carbocation + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–Br → Br
what the engine says happens: Heterolytic fission: the C1–Br bond breaks and both electrons go to Br, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. C1 becomes a tertiary carbocation.
explanation shown to students: Heterolytic fission: the C–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to the more electronegative bromine. A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by the three electron-releasing methyl groups (inductive effect), so it can form. This step is slow and sets the rate.

label: Protonated alcohol (an oxonium ion)
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → C1
what the engine says happens: O1's lone pair forms a bond to the positive C1: the nucleophile attacks the electrophile.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on water's oxygen forms a bond to the positive carbon. The carbocation is planar, so water can attack from either face: a chiral substrate gives a racemic mixture.

label: Products: 2-methylpropan-2-ol + H₃O⁺
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O2 → H; curly: bond O1–H → O1
what the engine says happens: O2 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–O1 bond breaks and both electrons go to O1, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: Proton transfer: a second water molecule uses a lone pair to take the H⁺, and the O–H bond's electrons return to the oxygen, which becomes neutral.

conditions: NaOH in ethanol; heat under reflux
label: Products: propene + water + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O → H; curly: bond C3–H → C3–C1; curly: bond C1–Br → Br
what the engine says happens: O uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). The C3–H bond's electrons move to form a C3–C1 π bond. Heterolytic fission: the C1–Br bond breaks and both electrons go to Br, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. Proton removal, C=C formation and loss of the leaving group happen in one step: an E2 elimination.
explanation shown to students: The hydroxide's lone pair takes a β-hydrogen as H⁺. The electrons of that C–H bond move between the two carbons to form the π bond, and the C–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to bromine. H and Br leave from opposite sides (anti-periplanar).

label: Secondary carbocation + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–H; curly: bond H–Br → Br
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to H: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. Heterolytic fission: the H–Br bond breaks and both electrons go to Br, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation.
explanation shown to students: The π bond is electron-rich, so the alkene acts as a nucleophile: its electrons form a bond to the δ+ hydrogen while the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically. Putting H on the CH₂ end leaves the positive charge on the middle carbon, a secondary carbocation, more stable than a primary one.

label: Product: 2-bromopropane
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Br → C2
what the engine says happens: Br's lone pair forms a bond to the positive C2: the nucleophile attacks the electrophile.
explanation shown to students: The bromide ion's lone pair bonds to the carbocation.

conditions: KCN, then dilute H⁺; room temperature
label: Alkoxide intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on C1 → C2; curly: bond C2–O → O
what the engine says happens: C1's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C2: C1 acts as a nucleophile. The C2=O π bond's electrons move onto O.
explanation shown to students: Oxygen is more electronegative, so the carbonyl carbon is δ+. Cyanide's carbon lone pair forms a C–C bond, and the C=O π bond's electrons move onto oxygen (carbon can't have five bonds), giving O⁻.

conditions: KCN, then dilute H⁺; room temperature
label: Product: 2-hydroxypropanenitrile + cyanide
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O → H; curly: bond H–C4 → C4
what the engine says happens: O uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–C4 bond breaks and both electrons go to C4, the more electronegative atom, which becomes an anion. C4 becomes a carbanion.
explanation shown to students: Proton transfer: an oxygen lone pair takes H⁺ from HCN, and the H–C bond's electrons go to carbon, regenerating CN⁻ (so cyanide acts as a catalyst).

label: Protonated alcohol (–OH₂⁺) + water
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → H2; curly: bond H2–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: O1 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H2–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on the alcohol's oxygen takes a proton from H₃O⁺ (the acid catalyst). The oxygen now carries a + charge, and the group can leave as a neutral water molecule, which is stable.

label: Tertiary carbocation + water
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: Heterolytic fission: the C1–O1 bond breaks and both electrons go to O1, the more electronegative atom. C1 becomes a tertiary carbocation.
explanation shown to students: Heterolytic fission: the C–O bond breaks with both electrons going to oxygen, and water leaves. This is the slow, rate-determining step; it happens because the tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three electron-releasing methyl groups.

label: Products: 2-methylpropene + H₃O⁺
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O3 → H1; curly: bond C2–H1 → C2–C1
what the engine says happens: O3 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). The C2–H1 bond's electrons move to form a C2–C1 π bond.
explanation shown to students: A water molecule takes a β-hydrogen as H⁺, and the electrons of the C–H bond move between the two carbons, forming the C=C and cancelling the + charge. The acid is regenerated as H₃O⁺, so it's a catalyst.

label: Carbocation + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–Br1; curly: bond Br1–Br2 → Br2
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to Br1: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. Heterolytic fission: the Br1–Br2 bond breaks and both electrons go to Br2, which leaves as an anion. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation.
explanation shown to students: The π electrons form a bond to the nearer, δ+ bromine, while the Br–Br bond's electrons move onto the far bromine, which leaves as Br⁻. The other carbon of the old C=C is left with a + charge (a secondary carbocation here).

label: Product: 2,3-dibromobutane
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Br2 → C2
what the engine says happens: Br2's lone pair forms a bond to the positive C2: the nucleophile attacks the electrophile.
explanation shown to students: The bromide's lone pair bonds to the carbocation, giving the 1,2-dibromo product: one bromine on each carbon of the old C=C.

label: Intermediate: the ring has lost its aromaticity
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–N; curly: bond N–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to N: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. The N=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation next to a C=C, so the positive charge is delocalised (resonance).
explanation shown to students: Two of the ring's π electrons form a C–N bond. Nitrogen can't take a fifth bond, so one N=O π bond's electrons move onto oxygen (O⁻, with N⁺: a nitro group). The positive charge is left in the ring, delocalised over three carbons; the ring is no longer aromatic, so this step is slow.

label: Products: nitrobenzene + H₂SO₄
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O3 → H; curly: bond C1–H → C1–C2
what the engine says happens: O3 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). The C1–H bond's electrons move to form a C1–C2 π bond.
explanation shown to students: HSO₄⁻ removes the H⁺, and the C–H bond's electrons go back into the ring, restoring the delocalised π system and regenerating H₂SO₄ (a catalyst).

label: Alkoxide intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on H1 → C1; curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: H1's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: H1 acts as a nucleophile. The C1=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1.
explanation shown to students: H⁻ uses its electron pair to bond to the carbonyl carbon. Carbon can't keep four bonds plus a new one, so the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, giving O⁻.

label: Product: propan-2-ol + OH⁻
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → H2; curly: bond H2–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: O1 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H2–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion.
explanation shown to students: Proton transfer: a lone pair on the alkoxide oxygen takes H⁺ from water, giving the alcohol and a hydroxide ion.

conditions: H₂O; room temperature (vigorous; steamy fumes of HCl)
label: Addition: tetrahedral intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O2 → C1; curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: O2's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: O2 acts as a nucleophile. The C1=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on water's oxygen bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen (O⁻). The carbon is briefly tetrahedral, bonded to four groups.

conditions: H₂O; room temperature (vigorous; steamy fumes of HCl)
label: Elimination: chloride leaves
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → O1–C1; curly: bond C1–Cl → Cl
what the engine says happens: O1's lone pair moves in between O1 and C1, making the O1=C1 double bond (a π bond). Heterolytic fission: the C1–Cl bond breaks and both electrons go to Cl, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. The C=O re-forms and pushes out the leaving group: the elimination half of addition–elimination.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on O⁻ re-forms the C=O π bond, and the C–Cl bond breaks with both electrons going to chlorine, which leaves as Cl⁻ (a good leaving group).

conditions: H₂O; room temperature (vigorous; steamy fumes of HCl)
label: Products: ethanoic acid + HCl
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Cl → H; curly: bond H–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: Cl uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: Chloride uses a lone pair to take H⁺ from the positive oxygen, giving the carboxylic acid and HCl, seen as steamy fumes.

label: Making the electrophile: Cl⁺ and AlCl₄⁻
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Cl2 → Al; curly: bond Cl1–Cl2 → Cl2
what the engine says happens: Cl2's lone pair forms a new Cl2–Al bond. Heterolytic fission: the Cl1–Cl2 bond breaks and both electrons go to Cl2.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on one chlorine forms a bond to aluminium (AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid, an electron-pair acceptor). That chlorine takes the Cl–Cl bond's electrons, so the other chlorine is left as Cl⁺, a strong electrophile.

label: Intermediate: the ring has lost its aromaticity
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–Cl1
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to Cl1: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation next to a C=C, so the positive charge is delocalised (resonance).
explanation shown to students: Two of the ring's delocalised π electrons form the C–Cl bond. The positive charge is spread over the remaining five carbons and the ring is no longer aromatic, so this step is slow.

label: Products: chlorobenzene + HCl, AlCl₃ regenerated
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond Cl2–Al → Cl2–H; curly: bond C1–H → C1–C2
what the engine says happens: The Cl2–Al bond's electrons move to form a Cl2–H bond. The C1–H bond's electrons move to form a C1–C2 π bond.
explanation shown to students: AlCl₄⁻ gives back a chloride: the electrons of an Al–Cl bond form the H–Cl bond, and the C–H bond's electrons return to the ring, restoring aromaticity. AlCl₃ is regenerated.

label: The acylium ion, CH₃CO⁺, and AlCl₄⁻
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Cl1 → Al; curly: bond C7–Cl1 → Cl1
what the engine says happens: Cl1's lone pair forms a new Cl1–Al bond. Heterolytic fission: the C7–Cl1 bond breaks and both electrons go to Cl1, the more electronegative atom. C7 becomes an acylium ion, R–C≡O⁺ ↔ R–C⁺=O: stabilised because the oxygen's lone pair can form a third bond to the carbon.
explanation shown to students: The chlorine's lone pair bonds to aluminium, and the C–Cl bond breaks with its electrons going to chlorine. Left behind is the acylium ion, stabilised because oxygen's lone pair can form a C≡O⁺ triple bond.

label: Intermediate: the ring has lost its aromaticity
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–C7
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to C7: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation next to a C=C, so the positive charge is delocalised (resonance).
explanation shown to students: A pair of the ring's π electrons forms a C–C bond to the acylium carbon; the positive charge moves into the ring.

label: Products: phenylethanone + HCl, AlCl₃ regenerated
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond Cl1–Al → Cl1–H; curly: bond C1–H → C1–C2
what the engine says happens: The Cl1–Al bond's electrons move to form a Cl1–H bond. The C1–H bond's electrons move to form a C1–C2 π bond.
explanation shown to students: An Al–Cl bond's electrons form H–Cl as the C–H bond's electrons return to the ring. Aromaticity is restored and AlCl₃ is regenerated.

label: Addition: tetrahedral intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O3 → C1; curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: O3's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: O3 acts as a nucleophile. The C1=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1.
explanation shown to students: Hydroxide's lone pair bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, giving O⁻. The carbon briefly has four single bonds.

label: Elimination: ethoxide leaves
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → O1–C1; curly: bond C1–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: O1's lone pair moves in between O1 and C1, making the O1=C1 double bond (a π bond). Heterolytic fission: the C1–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom, which keeps them and becomes negative. The C=O re-forms and pushes out the leaving group: the elimination half of addition–elimination.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on O⁻ re-forms the C=O, and the C–O bond to the ethyl group breaks, both electrons going to that oxygen: ethoxide leaves. The product so far is ethanoic acid.

label: Products: ethanoate ion + ethanol
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O2 → H; curly: bond O3–H → O3
what the engine says happens: O2 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–O3 bond breaks and both electrons go to O3, the more electronegative atom, which keeps them and becomes negative.
explanation shown to students: Proton transfer: ethoxide takes the acid's H⁺, giving ethanol and the ethanoate ion. The carboxylate can't be attacked by ethanol, so the reaction goes to completion. Acidifying afterwards gives the free carboxylic acid.

label: Addition: tetrahedral intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on N1 → C1; curly: bond C1–O → O
what the engine says happens: N1's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: N1 acts as a nucleophile. The C1=O π bond's electrons move onto O.
explanation shown to students: Nitrogen's lone pair bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Nitrogen now has four bonds and a + charge.

label: Elimination: chloride leaves
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O → O–C1; curly: bond C1–Cl → Cl
what the engine says happens: O's lone pair moves in between O and C1, making the O=C1 double bond (a π bond). Heterolytic fission: the C1–Cl bond breaks and both electrons go to Cl, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. The C=O re-forms and pushes out the leaving group: the elimination half of addition–elimination.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on O⁻ re-forms the C=O and the C–Cl bond breaks, chloride leaving with both electrons.

label: Products: ethanamide + NH₄⁺ (+ Cl⁻)
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on N2 → H; curly: bond N1–H → N1
what the engine says happens: N2 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–N1 bond breaks and both electrons go to N1, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: A second ammonia molecule acts as a base, taking H⁺ from the positive nitrogen: the products are ethanamide and ammonium chloride.

conditions: CH₃MgBr in dry ether, then H₃O⁺; room temperature
label: Alkoxide (as its magnesium salt)
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C4–Mg → C4–C1; curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: The C4–Mg bond's electrons move to form a C4–C1 bond. The C1=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1.
explanation shown to students: The C–Mg bond's electrons form a new bond from the methyl carbon to the carbonyl carbon; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen. Magnesium is left as MgBr⁺, paired with the alkoxide O⁻.

conditions: CH₃MgBr in dry ether, then H₃O⁺; room temperature
label: Product: 2-methylpropan-2-ol
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → H; curly: bond H–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: O1 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: Proton transfer: the alkoxide takes H⁺ from H₃O⁺, giving the tertiary alcohol.

mechanism: Making the electrophile: the nitronium ion (HNO₃ + H₂SO₄)
label: Protonated nitric acid + HSO₄⁻
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O3 → H2; curly: bond O4–H2 → O4
what the engine says happens: O3 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H2–O4 bond breaks and both electrons go to O4, the more electronegative atom, which keeps them and becomes negative.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on nitric acid's –OH oxygen takes H⁺ from sulfuric acid; the O–H bond's electrons stay on the sulfate oxygen, giving HSO₄⁻. Nitric acid is acting as a base here.

mechanism: Making the electrophile: the nitronium ion (HNO₃ + H₂SO₄)
label: Nitronium ion NO₂⁺ + water
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond N–O3 → O3; curly: lone pair on O2 → O2–N
what the engine says happens: Heterolytic fission: the N–O3 bond breaks and both electrons go to O3, the more electronegative atom. O2's lone pair moves in between O2 and N, making the O2=N double bond (a π bond). As the leaving group departs, the new π bond keeps N with a full outer shell.
explanation shown to students: The N–O bond breaks and water leaves with both electrons. A lone pair on the O⁻ forms a second N=O, giving the linear ion O=N⁺=O.

conditions: Br₂, FeBr₃ (or iron filings); room temperature, dry
label: Making the electrophile: Br⁺ and FeBr₄⁻
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Br2 → Fe; curly: bond Br1–Br2 → Br2
what the engine says happens: Br2's lone pair forms a new Br2–Fe bond. Heterolytic fission: the Br1–Br2 bond breaks and both electrons go to Br2.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on one bromine bonds to iron. That bromine keeps the Br–Br bond's electrons, so the other bromine is left as Br⁺.

conditions: Br₂, FeBr₃ (or iron filings); room temperature, dry
label: Intermediate: the ring has lost its aromaticity
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–Br1
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1=C2 bond form a bond to Br1: the electron-rich C=C acts as a nucleophile. C2 becomes a secondary carbocation next to a C=C, so the positive charge is delocalised (resonance).
explanation shown to students: Two of the ring's π electrons form the C–Br bond. The positive charge is delocalised over the other five ring carbons.

conditions: Br₂, FeBr₃ (or iron filings); room temperature, dry
label: Products: bromobenzene + HBr, FeBr₃ regenerated
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond Br2–Fe → Br2–H; curly: bond C1–H → C1–C2
what the engine says happens: The Br2–Fe bond's electrons move to form a Br2–H bond. The C1–H bond's electrons move to form a C1–C2 π bond.
explanation shown to students: An Fe–Br bond's electrons form H–Br as the C–H bond's electrons return to the ring. FeBr₃ is regenerated.

label: Vinyl cation + bromide
arrows (electron flow): curly: bond C1–C2 → C1–H; curly: bond H–Br → Br
what the engine says happens: The π electrons of the C1≡C2 bond form a bond to H: the electron-rich C≡C acts as a nucleophile. Heterolytic fission: the H–Br bond breaks and both electrons go to Br, the more electronegative atom, which leaves as an anion. C2 becomes a secondary vinyl cation (the + carbon is part of a C=C): less stable than an alkyl cation, which is why alkynes add electrophiles more slowly than alkenes.
explanation shown to students: Two of the triple bond's π electrons bond to the δ+ hydrogen of HBr, which loses bromide. H goes to the CH end, leaving the positive charge on the carbon with the methyl group.

label: Product: 2-bromopropene
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on Br → C2
what the engine says happens: Br's lone pair forms a bond to the positive C2: the nucleophile attacks the electrophile.
explanation shown to students: Bromide's lone pair bonds to the cation, giving 2-bromopropene. With excess HBr this adds again (Markovnikov), giving 2,2-dibromopropane.

mechanism: Acid hydrolysis: water + ethyl ethanoate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)
label: Protonated ester
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → H1; curly: bond H1–O3 → O3
what the engine says happens: O1 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H1–O3 bond breaks and both electrons go to O3, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen takes H⁺ from H₃O⁺. The positive charge makes the carbonyl carbon strongly δ+.

mechanism: Acid hydrolysis: water + ethyl ethanoate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)
label: Water adds: tetrahedral intermediate
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O4 → C1; curly: bond C1–O1 → O1
what the engine says happens: O4's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon C1: O4 acts as a nucleophile. The C1=O1 π bond's electrons move onto O1.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair on water bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move onto the (protonated) oxygen, which becomes neutral –OH.

mechanism: Acid hydrolysis: water + ethyl ethanoate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)
label: Proton transfer: ethoxy oxygen protonated
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O2 → H2; curly: bond O4–H2 → O4
what the engine says happens: O2 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H2–O4 bond breaks and both electrons go to O4, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: A proton moves from the water-derived oxygen to the ethoxy oxygen (in practice via solvent molecules). The ethoxy group can now leave as neutral ethanol.

mechanism: Acid hydrolysis: water + ethyl ethanoate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)
label: Ethanol leaves
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O1 → O1–C1; curly: bond C1–O2 → O2
what the engine says happens: O1's lone pair moves in between O1 and C1, making the O1=C1 double bond (a π bond). Heterolytic fission: the C1–O2 bond breaks and both electrons go to O2, the more electronegative atom. The C=O re-forms and pushes out the leaving group: the elimination half of addition–elimination.
explanation shown to students: A lone pair re-forms the C=O (protonated), and the C–O bond to the ethyl group breaks: ethanol leaves.

mechanism: Acid hydrolysis: water + ethyl ethanoate (H₃O⁺ catalyst)
label: Products: ethanoic acid + ethanol, H₃O⁺ regenerated
arrows (electron flow): curly: lone pair on O3 → H1; curly: bond O1–H1 → O1
what the engine says happens: O3 uses a lone pair to take a proton (H): it acts as a base (proton transfer). Heterolytic fission: the H1–O1 bond breaks and both electrons go to O1, the more electronegative atom.
explanation shown to students: Water takes the proton back, giving ethanoic acid and regenerating H₃O⁺, so the acid is a catalyst.

label: Initiation: two chlorine radicals
arrows (electron flow): fishhook: bond Cl1–Cl2 → Cl1; fishhook: bond Cl1–Cl2 → Cl2
what the engine says happens: Homolytic fission: the Cl1–Cl2 bond breaks with one electron going to each atom, making two radicals (initiation, often by UV light). Cl1 now has an unpaired electron: a radical. Cl2 now has an unpaired electron: a radical.
explanation shown to students: Homolytic fission: each chlorine takes one electron of the Cl–Cl bond. A fishhook (half-headed) arrow shows one electron moving, so you need two.

label: Propagation: HCl + methyl radical
arrows (electron flow): fishhook: lone pair on Cl2 → Cl2–H; fishhook: bond C–H → Cl2–H; fishhook: bond C–H → C
what the engine says happens: A radical attacks: its unpaired electron pairs with one from the bond it attacks, and the other electron is left on a new radical (propagation). C now has an unpaired electron: a radical.
explanation shown to students: The chlorine radical's electron pairs with one electron from the C–H bond to make H–Cl; the other C–H electron stays on carbon, which becomes a methyl radical. Three fishhooks.

label: Propagation: chloromethane + chlorine radical
arrows (electron flow): fishhook: lone pair on C → C–Cl3; fishhook: bond Cl3–Cl4 → C–Cl3; fishhook: bond Cl3–Cl4 → Cl4
what the engine says happens: A radical attacks: its unpaired electron pairs with one from the bond it attacks, and the other electron is left on a new radical (propagation). Cl4 now has an unpaired electron: a radical.
explanation shown to students: The methyl radical's electron pairs with one electron from Cl–Cl to make C–Cl; the other Cl gets the second electron and becomes a new chlorine radical, which carries the chain on.
